subject: BIM Basics
author: Anthony Hammond
title: What Is BIM? Building Information Modelling Explained
subHeading: Understanding the model, the information and the process
abstract: Discover how Building Information Modelling brings geometry, structured information and collaborative workflows together to support better project delivery.
body:
## Introduction

Building Information Modelling, usually shortened to BIM, is an approach to creating, managing and exchanging information about a built asset throughout its lifecycle. The asset might be a house, hospital, office building, bridge, road or water-treatment facility. BIM is often associated with three-dimensional models, but a model is only one part of the wider process. The real value comes from connecting useful information to the people, decisions and activities that need it.

## BIM is more than a 3D model

A conventional 3D model describes the shape of an object or building. A BIM model can also contain or reference information such as element type, dimensions, material, classification, specification, location, performance requirements and links to documents. A concrete pad footing, for example, may be represented geometrically in a structural model while also carrying an identifier, concrete specification and other properties required for design coordination or handover. Not every property belongs directly inside the model: some information may be held in schedules, drawings, databases, reports or linked information containers.

## A practical example: one pad footing

Imagine a six-storey reinforced-concrete office building. A column transfers loads into an isolated pad footing, which transfers those loads into the ground. To design and construct it, the project team needs coordinated information about the column grid, ground conditions, footing dimensions, reinforcement, concrete specification, setting-out coordinates and inspection requirements. The structural engineer develops design information; the contractor plans the work; the surveyor sets out the location; reinforcement specialists prepare and install the bars; and the concrete supplier provides the specified material and relevant records. BIM helps these people produce and exchange information in a coordinated way.

## Geometry, information and relationships

Three ideas help explain BIM. Geometry describes shape, size, position and spatial relationships. Information describes properties and requirements that are not necessarily visible in a view. Relationships connect elements to other elements, systems, documents or processes. A footing may be associated with a column, a level, a structural drawing, a reinforcement schedule and an inspection record. These connections help users understand not just what an element looks like, but what it is, where it belongs and what information is relevant to it.

## Collaboration and coordination

BIM supports collaboration by giving project participants a clearer basis for coordinating their work. Architectural, structural and building-services teams may create separate discipline models that are brought together for review. The team can identify inconsistent positions, conflicting geometry, missing information or unresolved design interfaces before these issues become expensive site problems. Coordination still requires professional judgement, clear responsibilities and timely communication. A software clash report does not decide how a conflict should be resolved, and a coordinated model does not automatically prove that a design is safe or compliant.

## BIM across the asset lifecycle

Information can be useful long after design and construction are complete. During early design, the team may need approximate geometry and options for comparison. During construction, it may need coordinated drawings, fabrication information, setting-out data and quality records. During operation, the owner may need verified asset identifiers, locations, specifications, warranties or maintenance information. The information required at each stage should be defined by its intended use. Creating information nobody needs adds effort; failing to create information that will later be essential can lead to costly investigation and reconstruction.

## BIM and software

BIM is not the name of a single software package. Applications such as Revit, Archicad, Tekla Structures, Civil 3D and specialist tools can support particular modelling and documentation tasks. Coordination tools can combine models for review, while open formats such as IFC can support information exchange between different applications. A project may use several platforms and still follow a coherent BIM process, provided the information requirements, responsibilities, exchange methods and quality checks are agreed.

## Common misconceptions

BIM does not simply mean drawing in 3D. It does not guarantee that every model is accurate, complete or coordinated. It does not mean every participant must use the same software, nor does it remove the need for drawings, specifications, calculations or site inspections. BIM is also not a substitute for contractual clarity or professional responsibility. Its effectiveness depends on the purpose of the information, the capability of the people producing it, the agreed processes and the discipline used to maintain it.

## Conclusion

The most useful way to understand BIM is to see it as an information-led way of working. The model is an important tool, but the objective is to make reliable information available to the people who need it, when they need it, in a form they can use. For the pad footing, success is not simply a detailed 3D object. Success is the right design, coordinated with the building, constructed from the correct information, checked on site and supported by the records required for future use.

## Practical test: does this information help someone?

Whenever a team proposes creating or adding information, it should ask what decision the information supports, who will use it, when it is needed and how it will be checked. This keeps the model focused on project outcomes. A concrete strength property is useful when it supports specification, checking or asset records; an arbitrary field with no agreed meaning is unlikely to help anyone.

## How teams keep information consistent

A model becomes more useful when participants agree what an element means and how its information is maintained. Two teams may use different software and still exchange useful information if element identifiers, coordinate systems, property definitions, revisions and responsibilities are clear. Without those agreements, apparently similar models may contain different assumptions or inconsistent values.

## The complete BIM workflow

The workflow includes requirements, planning, authoring, checking, sharing, coordination and delivery. Each step has a purpose. Requirements define the desired outcome; planning allocates work; authoring creates the information; checking assesses its quality; sharing enables coordination; and delivery provides information for the agreed use. The model supports this process but does not replace it.

## Practical consideration 1

A practical review should ask whether the element has a clear purpose, whether its information is coordinated with other disciplines, whether its properties are traceable to a reliable source, and whether the deliverables can be understood by intended users. The team should record assumptions and limitations rather than conceal them behind a polished visualisation.

## Practical consideration 2

A practical review should ask whether the element has a clear purpose, whether its information is coordinated with other disciplines, whether its properties are traceable to a reliable source, and whether the deliverables can be understood by intended users. The team should record assumptions and limitations rather than conceal them behind a polished visualisation.

subject: BIM Basics
author: Anthony Hammond
title: BIM Dimensions Explained: 3D, 4D, 5D and Beyond
subHeading: Connecting models with time, cost and asset information
abstract: Explore the commonly used BIM dimensions and learn how geometry, programme, cost and operational information can support project decisions.
body:
## Introduction

BIM dimensions are labels used to describe different kinds of information associated with a model or project workflow. Three-dimensional BIM concerns spatial geometry. Four-dimensional BIM commonly links model elements to time or programme information, while five-dimensional BIM commonly connects elements to quantities and cost. Further labels, including 6D and 7D, are used for topics such as sustainability, performance and facilities management, but their meanings vary between organisations and industry frameworks. These labels are useful shorthand, not a universally fixed set of formal ISO categories.

## 3D: geometry and spatial coordination

The foundation of most model-based workflows is three-dimensional geometry. Elements have shapes, dimensions and positions within a shared spatial reference. In a building model, columns, beams, slabs, walls and foundations can be examined in plan, section, elevation and 3D views. Geometry supports visualisation, design development, quantity extraction and coordination. It must still be modelled to an agreed purpose: a conceptual massing model and a construction-ready structural model require different levels of definition.

## 4D: connecting the model to time

Four-dimensional BIM usually links model objects or groups of objects to a construction programme. The programme contains activities, durations, dependencies and milestones; the model provides a spatial representation of what those activities relate to. Together, they can help teams visualise the intended construction sequence, investigate access constraints and communicate planned progress. For an RC frame, the footing, columns, beams and slabs can be associated with different construction activities. A 4D simulation is only as reliable as the programme, model mapping and assumptions behind it.

## 5D: quantities and cost

Five-dimensional BIM commonly refers to linking model information with quantities and cost data. A model may support quantity take-off for concrete volume, reinforcement quantities or areas of formwork. Those quantities can be connected to rates, cost codes, procurement packages or estimates. However, model quantities are not automatically equivalent to a tender or final account quantity. Measurement rules, waste allowances, temporary works, construction methods, exclusions and the reliability of model content must be understood. Cost professionals still need to review the basis of the estimate.

## 6D and 7D: performance and operation

Some organisations use 6D to describe sustainability, energy or performance analysis, and 7D to describe facilities management or asset information. Other frameworks assign these labels differently, so the number alone does not reliably explain what a deliverable contains. A more robust approach is to state the intended use directly. If a project requires operational data, specify the asset identifiers, attributes, documents, responsible parties and delivery format rather than simply asking for a '7D model'.

## Example: the pad footing

Consider one isolated footing beneath a column in a six-storey RC building. Its 3D representation communicates its geometry and location. A 4D link associates its excavation, blinding, reinforcement inspection, concrete pour and other activities with the programme. A 5D workflow may use its modelled dimensions to help calculate concrete volume and formwork quantities, subject to project measurement rules. Performance or operational information might include the footing identifier, location and approved construction records if those are required for the asset owner's future needs. Each additional information use needs a clear purpose.

## Data quality and limitations

Adding dimensions does not automatically improve a project. If a model element has the wrong dimensions, the associated quantity may be wrong. If programme activities are poorly defined, a simulation can give a misleading impression of the construction sequence. If cost codes are inconsistent, the estimate may be difficult to audit. Model-based outputs should therefore be checked against agreed assumptions, suitable source information and the responsible discipline's review process.

## Choosing the right information

A project should decide which uses genuinely add value. A small refurbishment may benefit from reliable 3D coordination without requiring a detailed 4D simulation. A complex phased project may gain significant value from programme-linked models. A cost planning team may need quantities and classification rather than a highly detailed visual model. An asset owner may prioritise a structured asset register over photorealistic geometry. The right combination depends on project scale, risk, procurement, client requirements and the decisions that must be made.

## Conclusion

BIM dimensions provide a convenient way to talk about connecting geometry with other information, but they should not replace precise requirements. Start by defining the question the team needs to answer, then decide what information, model links and checks are necessary. For the pad footing, the goal is not to claim that it is '7D'; the goal is to make geometry, sequence, quantities and relevant records useful to the people responsible for designing, building and managing the asset.

## Time and cost links need governance

Programme and cost links should be reviewed whenever the model or underlying assumptions change. If the footing dimensions change, quantities may need recalculation; if the construction sequence changes, the 4D simulation may need updating. The team should define who maintains the links and which source is authoritative for programme and cost. Otherwise, the visualisation can look precise while relying on outdated data.

## Dimensions are not a quality score

Calling a deliverable 4D or 5D does not prove that its data is complete or correct. A model can be linked to a programme without reflecting realistic work packages, and a quantity take-off can omit items that are not modelled. The dimensions describe connected information uses; they do not remove the need for validation, measurement rules and clear assumptions.

## Start with the decision

Before choosing a BIM dimension, identify the decision the team wants to improve. Is it sequencing pours, comparing design options, forecasting cost, planning maintenance or analysing energy performance? That question determines the necessary data and the people who need to participate. A targeted model-based workflow is often more useful than trying to attach every possible dimension to every project.

## Practical consideration 1

The team should record the basis of each calculation, the source of the programme link and the measurement method used for quantities. This makes outputs easier to audit and helps users understand the difference between a model-derived result and an accepted project quantity.

## Practical consideration 2

The team should record the basis of each calculation, the source of the programme link and the measurement method used for quantities. This makes outputs easier to audit and helps users understand the difference between a model-derived result and an accepted project quantity.

## Practical consideration 3

The team should record the basis of each calculation, the source of the programme link and the measurement method used for quantities. This makes outputs easier to audit and helps users understand the difference between a model-derived result and an accepted project quantity.

subject: BIM Basics
author: Anthony Hammond
title: What Is ISO 19650? The BIM Information Management Standard
subHeading: A practical introduction to information management across the asset lifecycle
abstract: Understand the purpose of the ISO 19650 series and how it helps project teams plan, produce, check and exchange built-asset information.
body:
## Introduction

ISO 19650 is a series of international standards concerned with the organisation and digitisation of information about buildings and civil engineering works, including building information modelling and information management using BIM. It provides a framework for managing information across the delivery and operational phases of assets. It is not a software manual and does not prescribe one universal modelling method. Instead, it establishes concepts, principles and processes that organisations can apply to suit their appointments and projects.

## Why a standard is useful

Construction projects involve organisations with different contracts, software, internal procedures and information needs. Without agreed processes, teams can use inconsistent file names, exchange outdated drawings, duplicate work or deliver information that is difficult to reuse. A shared information-management framework helps clarify what information is required, who is responsible for producing it, how it will be exchanged and how its status will be controlled. The standard provides a common language for these arrangements.

## Information management rather than software compliance

ISO 19650 should not be reduced to the question of whether a company uses Revit, a CDE platform or an IFC export. Software may support the process, but the standard's principles concern information requirements, responsibilities, planning, production, review, exchange and delivery. A team can use sophisticated tools and still manage information poorly if requirements and procedures are unclear. Conversely, the value of a well-defined process comes from consistent behaviour, not from a particular brand of software.

## The asset lifecycle

The ISO 19650 series addresses information management during both project delivery and asset operation. During delivery, the team creates and coordinates information needed to design and construct the asset. During operation, the owner or operator may need information to maintain, inspect, modify or manage the completed asset. The information requirements for these phases are related but not identical. Handover should therefore be planned rather than treated as a last-minute export exercise.

## Roles and appointments

The standard uses terms including appointing party, lead appointed party and appointed party. The appointing party establishes information needs and receives agreed deliverables. A lead appointed party manages information production and exchanges within its delivery team. Appointed parties provide information under their respective appointments. These are roles within appointment relationships, not universal job titles. The same organisation can perform different roles in different contractual relationships, and projects may contain multiple delivery teams.

## Requirements and planning

Information requirements should describe the information needed for a defined purpose, not simply request that a model be produced. Project teams may define exchange requirements, responsibilities, delivery milestones, formats, quality checks and acceptance processes. A BIM Execution Plan describes how the delivery team will approach the relevant requirements. Task and master information delivery plans help organise who will produce particular information and when it is due. The exact documents and arrangements should reflect the applicable standard, contract and project context.

## The Common Data Environment

The CDE is the agreed environment and workflow used to collect, manage and share information. It helps control information status, revisions and exchanges. The commonly described workflow states include Work in Progress, Shared, Published and Archived. Their purpose is to distinguish information being developed internally from information shared for coordination, information authorised for a particular use and information retained as a record. The CDE may be supported by software, but workflow, permissions and responsibilities must also be established.

## Example: an RC pad footing

Imagine the developer requires coordinated structural information and verified construction records for a footing. The structural engineer develops the design information, the main contractor coordinates the relevant supply-chain deliverables, and survey and concrete teams produce records within their scopes. ISO 19650 principles help the project define what is required, when it must be provided, how it will be identified, who checks it and how accepted information is handed over. The standard does not itself design the footing or replace the structural engineer's technical obligations.

## What ISO 19650 does not do

The standard does not guarantee that a design is safe, eliminate clashes, resolve contractual disputes or ensure that every model contains correct information. It does not replace building regulations, engineering codes, project specifications or professional judgement. Nor should the presence of a BIM Execution Plan be taken as proof that the whole process is being followed effectively. Implementation depends on suitable requirements, competent people, clear appointments and consistent execution.

## Conclusion

ISO 19650 offers a common framework for managing information so that project participants can work towards consistent outcomes. Its value lies in connecting information needs with responsibilities, planning, production, review, exchange and handover. For the pad footing, that means more than delivering a model: it means ensuring the correct design and construction information is available, identifiable, appropriately checked and suitable for its intended use.

## Standards and project documents work together

A standard provides a framework, while a project defines the detailed requirements and procedures needed for its circumstances. The appointment, project brief, information requirements, execution plan and CDE protocol should be consistent with each other. Teams should use the relevant editions and contractual documents rather than assume that one generic template automatically meets every requirement.

## Implementation requires people and checks

An information-management process works only when the people involved understand their responsibilities. Teams need suitable training, time to perform checks, clear escalation routes and realistic delivery milestones. Software configuration can support those arrangements, but it cannot compensate for unclear ownership or a culture in which outdated information continues to be used.

## Use the standard to clarify expectations

The project should translate the framework into practical instructions: what to produce, who checks it, how it is identified, when it is exchanged and how acceptance is recorded. Those practical decisions make the standard useful on site. A clear process also helps new team members understand the agreed approach without relying on informal explanations.

## Practical consideration 1

Project teams should check the current edition of the relevant standard and the guidance incorporated into their contract. Terms may evolve, and national guidance may explain implementation in a particular jurisdiction. Training material should distinguish general principles from project-specific procedures.

## Practical consideration 2

Project teams should check the current edition of the relevant standard and the guidance incorporated into their contract. Terms may evolve, and national guidance may explain implementation in a particular jurisdiction. Training material should distinguish general principles from project-specific procedures.

## Practical consideration 3

Project teams should check the current edition of the relevant standard and the guidance incorporated into their contract. Terms may evolve, and national guidance may explain implementation in a particular jurisdiction. Training material should distinguish general principles from project-specific procedures.

subject: BIM Basics
author: Anthony Hammond
title: BIM Levels Explained: Level 0, 1, 2 and 3
subHeading: Understanding the UK BIM maturity model and collaborative working
abstract: Learn what the familiar UK BIM maturity levels were intended to describe, how collaboration changes between approaches, and why these levels should be understood in context.
body:
## Introduction

The terms BIM Level 0, Level 1, Level 2 and Level 3 are widely encountered in discussions of BIM, particularly in the United Kingdom. They are associated with a historical maturity model used to describe increasing levels of digital information management and collaboration. They are not a universal grading system for every BIM project, nor are they the current ISO 19650 method for defining compliance. Understanding their original intent is useful, provided the terminology is not applied without context.

## Level 0: unmanaged or basic information exchange

Level 0 is commonly described as a basic approach relying largely on unmanaged CAD drawings and paper-based information exchange. Different parties may create their own drawings with limited structured collaboration. This does not mean every drawing is wrong or that the project cannot be delivered. It means the information process may depend heavily on manual coordination, document exchange and individual practices rather than a shared, structured approach.

## Level 1: managed CAD and structured information

Level 1 is commonly associated with managed CAD, standardised information structures and a controlled approach to drawing production and exchange. Information may be produced in 2D and 3D, but collaboration can remain largely based on exchanging files rather than working with a fully integrated project information process. Consistent naming, revision control and defined procedures can improve reliability even where discipline models remain separate.

## Level 2: collaborative BIM

In the historical UK model, Level 2 became associated with collaborative BIM in which separate discipline models and information sources are developed by different parties and coordinated through agreed exchanges. Participants do not necessarily work in one shared native model or use identical software. Instead, they share information in agreed formats, coordinate models, and follow common information-management processes. Open formats such as IFC may support exchange where appropriate, alongside native formats and other deliverables.

## Level 3: more integrated information

Level 3 was used in the historical maturity model to describe a more integrated approach to information sharing and collaboration, often associated with connected data and shared models or environments. The precise meaning and implementation of Level 3 have varied in industry discussion. It should not be treated as a single universal technical specification that every project can simply achieve by adopting one platform.

## Example: the same pad footing at different maturity levels

Imagine an RC building with a pad footing beneath a column. In a basic unmanaged workflow, the structural engineer may issue a drawing and the contractor may circulate printed copies, with updates communicated manually. In a more managed workflow, drawings have consistent identifiers and revisions, and the team controls which version is current. In a collaborative model-based workflow, the structural model can be coordinated with the architectural model, relevant information is exchanged through agreed processes, and issues are tracked to resolution. More integrated approaches may connect information more directly to programme, cost or asset systems. These are illustrative differences, not formal acceptance criteria for each level.

## Maturity is not the same as model detail

A highly detailed 3D model does not automatically represent a mature BIM process. A team could model every bar in a footing but still fail to control revisions, agree responsibilities or deliver useful handover data. Another team may use a relatively simple model but have clear information requirements, reliable exchange procedures and strong coordination. Maturity concerns how information is managed and used, not just how visually complex a model appears.

## The relationship with ISO 19650

ISO 19650 provides a framework for information management using BIM, but it does not define a simple Level 0 to Level 3 ladder as a universal compliance rating. Modern projects should focus on their information requirements, appointments, delivery plans, CDE workflows and defined information exchanges. The historical levels can help explain how industry thinking developed, but project requirements should use clear, current language rather than rely on a maturity label alone.

## How to describe a project accurately

Instead of saying only that a project is 'Level 2 BIM', describe what actually happens. For example: discipline models are developed separately; model exchanges occur at defined milestones; the project uses a CDE with revision and status control; coordination issues are assigned and tracked; and handover information is checked against stated requirements. This description gives clients and team members a more actionable understanding of the workflow.

## Conclusion

The BIM maturity levels are useful historical context for understanding the move from basic digital drafting towards managed and collaborative information production. They should not be confused with model detail, software capability or ISO 19650 compliance. The practical question is whether the project has clear information requirements, suitable processes, competent people and reliable exchanges. Those are the factors that make information useful for the pad footing and for the wider building.

## Use maturity labels carefully

Maturity models can help teams discuss capability and identify areas for improvement, but a label is a simplification. It cannot describe every aspect of a project's data quality, collaboration, security or delivery process. When comparing projects, examine actual procedures and outcomes rather than relying only on the number assigned to a maturity level.

## A practical maturity checklist

Useful questions include whether information requirements are defined; whether roles and deliverables are clear; whether models use agreed coordinates; whether revisions are controlled; whether coordination issues have owners; whether information is checked before issue; and whether handover requirements are planned. These questions reveal more about practical capability than a maturity label alone.

## Collaboration is an organisational behaviour

Collaborative BIM depends on people sharing appropriate information, raising issues early and respecting agreed responsibilities. A federated model can support this behaviour, but it does not create it automatically. Teams need communication routines, decision records and a reliable way to resolve disagreements. Technology is an enabler, not a replacement for collaboration.

## Practical consideration 1

A useful review also examines whether the project can trace a decision back to the information used, whether participants understand which model is authoritative for each purpose and whether the team has a consistent method for handling changes. These behaviours show how well the process functions.

## Practical consideration 2

A useful review also examines whether the project can trace a decision back to the information used, whether participants understand which model is authoritative for each purpose and whether the team has a consistent method for handling changes. These behaviours show how well the process functions.

subject: BIM Basics
author: Anthony Hammond
title: LOD Explained: Level of Detail, Level of Development and LoIN
subHeading: Choosing the right model information for the intended purpose
abstract: Understand how LOD terminology is used, why definitions vary, and how Level of Information Need helps teams specify geometry, data and documentation.
body:
## Introduction

LOD is one of the most commonly used terms in BIM, but it can also be one of the most confusing. Depending on the framework, LOD may refer to Level of Detail, Level of Development or a defined combination of geometry and information reliability. Different standards and industry guides use different definitions and scales. As a result, a project should identify the framework it follows rather than assume that every participant interprets an LOD number in the same way.

## Level of Detail and Level of Development

Level of Detail is often used to describe how much geometric detail is shown in a model element. Level of Development, in frameworks that use that term, communicates the extent to which an element's geometry and associated information can be relied upon for specified uses. These ideas are related but not identical. A visually elaborate element may still be based on assumptions and may not be suitable for construction or fabrication. The label must be interpreted according to the project's chosen definition.

## Why more detail is not always better

Detailed modelling requires time, increases file size and can make changes more expensive. If an early design decision only needs an approximate footing footprint and depth, modelling every reinforcement bar may not improve the decision. Conversely, a reinforcement detailer may need accurate bar geometry and schedules for fabrication. The right model content depends on the purpose, the stage of the project and the decisions the information must support.

## Level of Information Need

Level of Information Need, commonly abbreviated LoIN, is a purpose-led approach for defining how much information is required for a particular use and at a particular time. ISO 7817-1:2024 provides a framework for this concept. It considers geometrical information, alphanumerical information and documentation. Instead of requesting an unspecified level of detail, the team identifies the geometry, properties and supporting documents that are necessary for the task.

## Geometrical information

Geometrical information includes shape, size, position, orientation and spatial relationships. For a pad footing, the required geometry may include its length, width, depth, level and position relative to a grid and column. Depending on the use, the model may also need reinforcement layout, cover zones or relationships with connected elements. The required geometric definition should be sufficient for the intended task without introducing unsupported precision.

## Alphanumerical information

Alphanumerical information includes properties and values associated with an element. A footing may require an element identifier, type, concrete specification, classification code or references to relevant design documents. Which properties are necessary depends on the information requirement. A model should not be filled with arbitrary parameters simply to appear information-rich; each property should have a clear purpose and a reliable source.

## Documentation

Documentation includes drawings, schedules, reports, certificates, photographs and other records needed to support a task. Some information is better represented in a drawing or report than as a model parameter. For the footing, structural calculations and inspection records may be essential even if they are linked to the model rather than embedded within it. The team should define how these documents are identified, associated and delivered.

## A footing through different stages

At feasibility stage, approximate footing dimensions and location may be enough to compare options. During detailed design, the model and documents may need coordinated dimensions, design properties and references to calculations. For construction, the team may require approved drawings, reinforcement details and setting-out data. At handover, verified as-built information and selected construction records may be required. The information changes because the purpose changes; the model does not simply become more detailed in every possible way.

## Specifying information requirements clearly

A useful requirement states what information is needed, for which element or system, by whom, for what purpose and at what milestone. It should also define applicable units, classification, accuracy, format and acceptance criteria. If a client asks for 'LOD 400' without identifying the framework or required deliverables, different teams may make different assumptions. Clear examples and schedules reduce ambiguity.

## Quality and responsibility

The requested level of information does not itself guarantee accuracy. The responsible author must produce and check information according to the appointment and applicable technical obligations. Model users should understand whether information is preliminary, coordinated, approved for a particular use or verified as built. A high LOD label should never be interpreted as automatic proof that an element is designed, checked or ready for fabrication.

## Conclusion

LOD terminology can be useful when a project has agreed definitions, but it is not a substitute for a clear statement of information needs. LoIN encourages teams to define the geometry, data and documentation required for a purpose. For the pad footing, the best model is not the one with the most detail; it is the one that contains the right, reliable information for the design, construction or operational decision being made.

## Visual appearance is not reliability

A model can look detailed while containing guessed dimensions, unverified properties or geometry that is unsuitable for fabrication. Conversely, a simplified model can be reliable for a specific early-stage decision. Users should understand the status and purpose of information before relying on it. Model views should not imply certainty beyond what the author has established.

## A practical information requirement

A clear requirement might state that the footing model must include its unique identifier, design dimensions, level, material specification and relationship to the relevant column, and that approved drawings and specified records must be delivered before a defined milestone. This is more actionable than requesting a generic LOD without defining the governing framework or intended use.

## Plan for change

Design develops over time, and the required information changes as decisions become more certain. The team should define when information is expected, what review it must pass and how changes are communicated. A requirement should avoid demanding premature precision while ensuring construction-critical information is available before work depends on it.

## Practical consideration 1

Where the model is used for fabrication or construction, the required information should be agreed with the people who will rely on it. Their needs may include tolerances, interfaces, access, schedules or supporting documents that are not obvious from a general-purpose model view.

## Practical consideration 2

Where the model is used for fabrication or construction, the required information should be agreed with the people who will rely on it. Their needs may include tolerances, interfaces, access, schedules or supporting documents that are not obvious from a general-purpose model view.

subject: BIM Basics
author: Anthony Hammond
title: What Is a CDE? Common Data Environments Explained
subHeading: Managing information, revisions and exchanges across a project
abstract: Learn how a Common Data Environment combines information-management workflows with technology to help project teams control and exchange reliable information.
body:
## Introduction

A Common Data Environment, or CDE, is the agreed environment and workflow used to collect, manage and share information for a project or asset. It is central to many BIM information-management processes because construction projects generate large quantities of models, drawings, schedules, specifications, reports and records. The CDE helps teams identify information, understand its status and revision, and exchange it through a controlled process.

## A CDE is more than a folder

It is tempting to think of a CDE as a shared drive, cloud folder or software platform. Those technologies may form part of the solution, but a CDE also requires defined processes and responsibilities. The team needs to agree who can upload, review, authorise and publish information; how revisions are managed; how suitability is communicated; and how superseded information is retained. A platform without an agreed workflow can simply make confusion available to more people.

## The common workflow states

The familiar ISO 19650 CDE workflow includes Work in Progress, Shared, Published and Archived. Work in Progress contains information being developed within a task team's own working environment. Shared information is made available to others for coordination or another defined purpose. Published information has passed the required authorisation process for a specified use. Archived information is retained as a record of the information's history and status. The exact configuration should follow the project's agreed procedure.

## Status is not just a colour

A model or drawing needs to communicate what it is suitable for. A file shared for coordination should not automatically be treated as authorised for construction. Likewise, a published design drawing may be superseded by a later revision. The CDE process should make the status, revision and permitted use clear. Users must still check the relevant metadata and project rules rather than relying on a colour, folder name or informal message.

## Information containers and identifiers

A CDE manages identifiable information containers, such as models, drawings, schedules, reports and other files. Containers need appropriate identifiers and metadata so that users can locate and distinguish them. Naming conventions can identify the project, originator, volume or system, level, type and other agreed fields. The exact naming structure depends on project requirements and applicable conventions. Consistency is more important than inventing a complex naming system nobody follows.

## Example: a changed footing detail

Suppose the structural engineer revises the reinforcement arrangement for a pad footing after a coordination review. The engineer updates the model and drawing in its work area, checks the revision, then shares the information for coordination. The relevant team reviews it and the project follows its authorisation procedure before the information is released for construction. The previous version remains identifiable and is no longer mistaken for the current approved information. The site team can then work from the correct revision, subject to the project's controls.

## Review and issue resolution

A CDE supports review, but it does not replace technical checking. The structural engineer remains responsible for the checks allocated to its design scope. The contractor coordinates construction information and identifies interfaces. Other parties review information for their own purposes. Comments, issues and decisions should be recorded in a way that allows the team to see who is responsible, what action is required and whether it has been resolved.

## Security and access

Projects may contain commercially sensitive, personal, security-related or otherwise restricted information. A CDE should apply appropriate access permissions and information-security measures. Not every participant needs access to every container. Permissions should support collaboration while protecting information and ensuring that changes are attributable to the relevant users. Security arrangements should be proportionate to the project's risks and requirements.

## CDE and handover

Handover should be planned from the beginning. The team needs to know which information containers must be delivered, in what format, with what metadata and which checks. Information should not be assumed complete merely because files have been uploaded. The receiving party may need to verify required fields, references, status and suitability for the intended operational use. A clear handover process reduces the risk of losing important records after construction.

## Conclusion

A well-managed CDE gives the project a controlled way to identify, review, share and retain information. Its value comes from the combination of technology, workflow, responsibilities and consistent use. For the pad footing, this helps ensure that the current design, construction information and final records are available to the right people without confusing drafts, coordination exchanges and authorised deliverables.

## Revision control protects site decisions

A revision identifies a version of an information container, but users also need to understand its status and suitability. A newer draft is not automatically authorised for construction. The project process should make it clear which version supersedes which, who approved it for a particular use and how site teams are informed of changes.

## The CDE is a workflow across organisations

Different organisations may use different internal systems, but they need an agreed way to exchange and manage project information. The CDE process defines how information passes between working, shared, published and archived states. It should specify permissions, review steps, metadata and responsibilities so that every participant can understand the information's current status.

## Measure success by usability

A CDE is successful when people can find the correct information, understand its status and use it for the task they are authorised to perform. Upload counts and storage capacity are not good measures of information quality. Useful checks include whether naming is consistent, revisions are clear, required metadata is present and superseded information is not mistaken for current deliverables.

## Practical consideration 1

The project should test the workflow using a real information exchange before relying on it at scale. A trial can reveal whether users understand status codes, whether notifications reach the right people and whether the receiving team can identify the current deliverable without guesswork.

## Practical consideration 2

subject: BIM Basics
author: Anthony Hammond
title: BIM Planning Documents: EIR, BEP, MIDP and TIDP
subHeading: Defining information requirements, responsibilities and delivery dates
abstract: Explore the main information requirements and planning documents used in BIM and how they help project teams agree what will be delivered, by whom and when.
body:
## Introduction

BIM projects need more than models and drawings. Before information can be produced consistently, the team needs to understand what is required, why it is required, who will produce it, how it will be checked and when it must be delivered. Several information-management documents help establish these arrangements. Common terms include EIR, BEP, MIDP and TIDP, alongside broader organisational, asset and project information requirements.

## Information requirements start with a purpose

Information requirements should be connected to decisions and outcomes. An owner may need information to approve a design, coordinate construction, assess cost or operate the completed asset. Requirements become useful when they identify the relevant information, the party responsible, the required milestone, the format and the acceptance criteria. A request for a detailed model without a defined purpose can lead to unnecessary work or leave critical deliverables unspecified.

## OIR, AIR and PIR

Organisational Information Requirements, Asset Information Requirements and Project Information Requirements describe different contexts for information needs. OIR concern information needed to support an organisation's objectives. AIR concern information needed to operate and manage an asset. PIR concern information needed to make decisions and deliver a project. The relationship between them depends on the organisation, asset and project. They should not be treated as interchangeable labels or as a universal checklist that every project must copy without adaptation.

## EIR: Exchange Information Requirements

Exchange Information Requirements define information to be exchanged by an appointed party for a stated purpose and at specified points. They may address deliverables, formats, timing, responsibilities, required properties, quality checks and acceptance. Their exact form depends on the appointment and project arrangements. The critical point is that the receiving party should communicate what is needed clearly enough for the providing party to plan and deliver it.

## BEP: BIM Execution Plan

The BIM Execution Plan describes how the delivery team intends to meet the relevant information-management requirements. It can set out roles, responsibilities, methods, standards, software and exchange formats, coordination procedures, quality assurance and proposed delivery arrangements. A pre-appointment BEP may explain a prospective team's approach during procurement. After appointment, the approach is confirmed and developed for the actual project. The BEP should be a usable plan, not a document produced only to satisfy a tender checklist.

## TIDP: Task Information Delivery Plan

A Task Information Delivery Plan sets out the information deliverables associated with a task team, including what it will produce and when. For a structural design team, this could include the structural model, footing drawings, calculations, reinforcement information and scheduled review dates. The plan helps the team coordinate dependencies and ensure that deliverables are available when other work relies on them.

## MIDP: Master Information Delivery Plan

The Master Information Delivery Plan consolidates the relevant task team delivery plans for the delivery team. It gives the team an overall view of the information deliverables, responsibilities and dates. The main contractor may use the combined plan to coordinate structural design, architectural information, survey data, subcontractor details and construction records. It helps expose dependencies, such as the need for an approved footing design before reinforcement detailing or setting out can proceed.

## Example: planning one pad footing

The developer requires coordinated design information and selected as-built records. The structural engineer is responsible for the footing design deliverables within its appointment. The main contractor needs the approved design information before sequencing the work and arranging relevant subcontractors. The surveyor requires reliable coordinates and levels. The reinforcement detailer needs the correct design and detailing requirements. The concrete supplier needs the specified concrete requirements and delivery arrangements. EIR and planning documents can make these dependencies visible and assign dates and responsibilities.

## Planning, checking and acceptance

Planning documents should identify not only when information is due but also how it will be reviewed and accepted. The author may need to perform internal checks before sharing a model. Other teams may review interfaces and raise issues. The receiving party may have acceptance criteria for the final deliverable. Clear responsibilities reduce the chance that an information exchange is treated as complete simply because a file was uploaded.

## Common mistakes

One common mistake is using the BEP as a generic manual without connecting it to actual deliverables. Another is creating a delivery schedule with dates but no clear dependencies or responsible parties. Teams may also confuse the EIR with the BEP, or assume that the master plan replaces the individual task team's own planning. Documents should be consistent with the appointments, proportionate to project complexity and updated when agreed requirements or delivery arrangements change.

## Conclusion

Information requirements explain what is needed and why; the BEP explains how the team intends to meet those requirements; the TIDP plans deliverables for a task team; and the MIDP brings delivery plans together. Terminology and contractual arrangements should be checked against the applicable ISO 19650 guidance and project requirements. For the footing, effective planning helps ensure that design, reinforcement, survey, construction and handover information arrives in the right sequence.

## Dependencies matter as much as dates

A delivery date is meaningful only when the team understands the information needed before work can start. Reinforcement detailing may depend on an agreed structural design; setting out depends on reliable coordinates; and concrete ordering depends on the specified requirements and construction plan. Delivery plans should expose these dependencies so that late inputs can be addressed before they disrupt site work.

## Documents must reflect the actual appointment

A template should never be copied into a project without checking who appoints whom and what each party has agreed to deliver. Roles, formats and acceptance criteria should align with contractual obligations. If the appointment changes, the relevant plans may need updating so that responsibilities and delivery dates remain realistic.

## A plan needs active management

The TIDP and MIDP should be used during the project, not filed away after mobilisation. The team can review upcoming deliverables, identify late inputs, record changes and agree recovery actions. Regular review makes the plan a practical management tool and helps prevent downstream teams from working from incomplete or superseded information.

## Practical consideration 1

Delivery plans should allow time for authoring, internal checking, coordination review, responses to comments and final issue. Treating the production date as the same as the acceptance date can create unrealistic expectations and leave no time to resolve problems.

## Practical consideration 2

Delivery plans should allow time for authoring, internal checking, coordination review, responses to comments and final issue. Treating the production date as the same as the acceptance date can create unrealistic expectations and leave no time to resolve problems.

subject: BIM Basics
author: Anthony Hammond
title: Who Does What in BIM? Appointing Party, Lead Appointed Party and Appointed Party
subHeading: Understanding roles, appointments and information responsibilities
abstract: Understand the key ISO 19650 role terms and how information responsibilities cascade from a client through designers, contractors and suppliers.
body:
## Introduction

BIM projects involve organisations with different responsibilities. The developer may define project outcomes, the architect develops architectural information, the structural engineer designs the frame, the main contractor coordinates construction, and specialist suppliers and subcontractors provide products, services and records. ISO 19650 uses the terms appointing party, lead appointed party and appointed party to describe roles in information-management relationships. These terms do not simply map to job titles.

## The appointing party

The appointing party is the organisation or party that establishes information needs and receives the agreed information deliverables from the party it appoints. In our example, the developer may be the appointing party when it directly appoints the architect, structural engineer or main contractor. It defines the information needed for project decisions and asset handover. The developer does not necessarily produce all the technical information itself; it establishes requirements and receives the agreed outputs.

## The lead appointed party

The lead appointed party manages information production and exchanges within its delivery team in accordance with its appointment. A main contractor may perform this role for its construction delivery team when appointed by the developer. It coordinates relevant information from designers, subcontractors and suppliers and plans the exchanges needed to deliver its scope. An architect or another consultant can also be a lead appointed party within its own appointment and delivery-team arrangement.

## The appointed party

An appointed party provides information under an appointment. The structural engineering consultant may be an appointed party when directly appointed by the developer or by another organisation. A geotechnical consultant provides ground information; a reinforcement detailer prepares agreed detailing outputs; a surveyor provides setting-out or as-built information; and suppliers provide relevant product and delivery records. Whether a party is formally an appointed party depends on the actual appointment and information responsibilities, not just its trade.

## Project team, delivery team and task team

The project team is the wider group of parties involved in delivering the project. A delivery team consists of a lead appointed party and its appointed parties. A task team is a group of people organised to perform a particular task, such as structural modelling, reinforcement detailing or surveying. These groupings describe different scopes of collaboration and should not be confused with the contractual role labels.

## Example: the information cascade for one footing

A developer identifies the information required for an isolated pad footing beneath a column. The architect provides the layout, grid and levels within its scope. The geotechnical consultant supplies ground investigation information. The structural engineer uses the relevant inputs to design the footing and produces calculations and drawings. The main contractor coordinates the construction information required from its delivery team. The reinforcement detailer prepares the required bar details, the surveyor sets out the location, the concrete producer supplies the specified mix and records, and the construction team records relevant inspections and as-built information.

## Information flows in multiple directions

Requirements commonly flow from the appointing party into the relevant appointments. Technical information then moves between designers, contractors and suppliers as the project develops. Site observations, survey results, change requests and construction records can flow back to designers or to the party coordinating the information. The process is therefore not a simple one-way hierarchy. The CDE and agreed communication procedures help teams identify which information is current, who needs it and what action is required.

## Design responsibility is not the same as information coordination

A main contractor may coordinate the information needed for construction without automatically becoming responsible for the structural engineer's design. The structural engineer's technical duties depend on its appointment and applicable professional obligations. Similarly, a detailer may prepare reinforcement drawings within an agreed scope without assuming every aspect of the structural design. Responsibilities must be established contractually and technically rather than inferred from a BIM role label.

## Multiple lead appointed parties

A project may contain more than one lead appointed party, each responsible for its own delivery team and appointment. The architect and main contractor may both be directly appointed by the developer and manage different information scopes. Alternatively, the structural engineer may be appointed through the architect or directly by the contractor. These arrangements affect the information relationships, so the actual appointment structure must be examined before assigning the terms.

## Conclusion

The three core terms clarify who establishes information needs, who manages information production within a delivery team and who provides information under an appointment. They are relational roles, not fixed job titles. For the footing, understanding these roles helps the team assign information responsibilities while preserving the distinction between coordination, technical design and construction obligations.

## Appointment relationships should be mapped

A simple responsibility matrix can show which party appoints each organisation, which information each party produces and who receives it. The matrix should distinguish authoring, checking, coordination, approval and acceptance where these responsibilities differ. It can help avoid assuming that the person who uploads a model is also responsible for its technical content.

## Suppliers contribute information too

Suppliers and subcontractors may provide product data, certificates, delivery records, fabrication details and as-built information. These outputs should be defined where they are needed and proportionate to the appointment. The main contractor may coordinate their delivery, but the specific party responsible for each record must be clear.

## Information exchange does not remove professional duties

BIM processes support communication and traceability, but they do not replace professional judgement, design checking or contractual duties. A model review may reveal a discrepancy, yet the responsible designer must determine the appropriate technical response within its scope. The project should preserve clear approval and change-control processes.

## Practical consideration 1

A responsibility matrix should be consistent with appointment documents and updated when scope or procurement changes. It should also identify who has authority to approve changes and who is responsible for communicating them to other affected teams.

## Practical consideration 2

A responsibility matrix should be consistent with appointment documents and updated when scope or procurement changes. It should also identify who has authority to approve changes and who is responsible for communicating them to other affected teams.

## Practical consideration 3

A responsibility matrix should be consistent with appointment documents and updated when scope or procurement changes. It should also identify who has authority to approve changes and who is responsible for communicating them to other affected teams.

subject: BIM Basics
author: Anthony Hammond
title: Federated Models and Clash Detection Explained
subHeading: Coordinating architecture, structure and building services
abstract: Learn how discipline models are combined for coordination, what clash detection can reveal, and how teams turn model issues into resolved design decisions.
body:
## Introduction

Most complex building projects are not designed by one person working in one model. Architects, structural engineers and building-services designers develop information for different disciplines and systems. A federated model brings selected discipline models together in a coordinated environment for review. Clash detection can help identify potential conflicts, but the real objective is to resolve design and construction issues, not simply produce a report full of coloured markers.

## Discipline models

A discipline model represents information developed by a particular team or for a defined scope. An architectural model may contain walls, doors, spaces and finishes. A structural model may contain foundations, columns, beams, slabs and structural walls. Mechanical, electrical and plumbing models may contain ducts, pipes, cable trays and equipment. The content and responsibility for each model should be agreed so that the models work together without unnecessary duplication or gaps.

## What is model federation?

Federation is the process of bringing separate models or information sources together for coordination and review. The models may remain authored in different applications and owned by different organisations. Their alignment depends on agreed coordinates, levels, orientation, units and exchange procedures. If the models are positioned incorrectly, a coordination review can identify false clashes or miss real ones. Model federation therefore begins with checking that the inputs are suitable and correctly aligned.

## Hard clashes

A hard clash occurs when modelled objects physically intersect in a way that may be unintended. A duct passing through a structural beam without a designed opening is a typical example. A pipe may intersect a column or a reinforcement bar may overlap another bar in a physically impossible arrangement. Not every geometric intersection is automatically an error: some elements are intended to connect, overlap or be embedded. The team must interpret each result in context.

## Soft clashes and clearance issues

A soft clash concerns a required clearance, tolerance, access zone or other spatial constraint rather than a simple physical intersection. A maintenance zone may need to remain clear in front of equipment. A pipe may need sufficient space for insulation or installation. A steel fixer may need access to install and tie reinforcement. These requirements need explicit rules or agreed review criteria; a clash tool cannot infer every clearance requirement correctly from geometry alone.

## Other coordination issues

Some important issues are not straightforward geometric clashes. They may involve inconsistent levels, missing openings, inadequate access, conflicting construction sequences, incomplete information or mismatched element identifiers. A useful coordination process combines model-based checks with drawing reviews, design discussions and knowledge of construction methods. Automated detection can narrow attention to likely problems, but professional judgement remains essential.

## Example: the pad footing

Suppose a building-services drainage pipe passes close to an RC pad footing. The federated model may reveal that the pipe conflicts with the footing or its required excavation zone. The structural engineer, drainage designer and contractor must review the issue, establish the design constraints and agree a solution. No change should be made without the responsible designers and project procedures. Another example is reinforcement congestion around column starter bars, where a model review can reveal a detailing problem before the pour.

## Issue management

A clash report is a starting point, not a complete coordination process. Each issue should have a clear description, location, responsible party, priority or severity where appropriate, status and target date. The team records the proposed action, reviews the revised information and verifies that the issue has been resolved. Duplicate or irrelevant clashes should be filtered out so that the team focuses on meaningful issues. Clear issue ownership prevents problems from being repeatedly discussed without progress.

## Model quality and tolerances

Clash results depend on model quality, element classification, geometry, tolerances and test settings. A model may contain simplified geometry that does not represent fabrication details. Two elements may appear to overlap because of a modelling convention, or a small intersection may be acceptable within the design. Conversely, an apparently clear model may hide an installation or maintenance problem not represented in the geometry. Coordination checks should be defined for the intended purpose and supplemented by appropriate review.

## Coordination and responsibility

The person who detects an issue is not necessarily the person authorised to resolve it. A contractor may identify a conflict and coordinate a resolution, while the relevant design consultant remains responsible for its design decisions. Changes must be communicated to affected parties and incorporated into the correct information containers through the agreed revision and authorisation process. The team should not treat a clash as resolved until the agreed action has been implemented and verified.

## Conclusion

Federated models and clash detection help teams find coordination problems earlier, communicate them clearly and track their resolution. Their effectiveness depends on reliable source models, agreed coordinates, meaningful tests, clear responsibilities and disciplined issue management. For the footing, the goal is not a zero-clash screenshot at any cost; it is a buildable, coordinated solution supported by information the project team can trust.

## Prioritise issues by impact

A coordination report may contain hundreds of potential intersections. The team should distinguish meaningful design or construction risks from intentional connections, modelling artefacts and low-priority issues. Prioritisation can consider safety, cost, programme, access, rework and the point at which a decision is needed. Clear issue descriptions help the responsible team act quickly.

## Use agreed coordinates and model versions

A federated review is only meaningful when the input models align and their versions are known. The team should check coordinate systems, units, orientation, levels, model scope and status before running tests. It should also record which model versions were used for a review so that results can be traced and repeated when necessary.

## Close the loop after a change

When a designer revises an element, the team should update the relevant information containers, communicate the revision and rerun necessary checks. A comment marked 'resolved' is not enough if the model or drawing has not been updated. Verification closes the loop between detecting a problem and delivering a coordinated solution.

## Practical consideration 1

The coordination team should agree what counts as a clash, which tolerances apply and which element categories should be tested. These rules help reduce false positives and make results repeatable. Test settings should be documented so the team can understand why a result was generated.

## Practical consideration 2

The coordination team should agree what counts as a clash, which tolerances apply and which element categories should be tested. These rules help reduce false positives and make results repeatable. Test settings should be documented so the team can understand why a result was generated.

subject: BIM Basics
author: Anthony Hammond
title: PIM vs AIM: BIM Across the Asset Lifecycle
subHeading: From project delivery information to operational asset information
abstract: Discover how the Project Information Model and Asset Information Model serve different purposes and how information can be prepared for handover and operation.
body:
## Introduction

A built asset generates and uses information before, during and after construction. The Project Information Model, commonly abbreviated PIM, relates to information developed and used to deliver a project. The Asset Information Model, or AIM, relates to information needed to operate and manage the completed asset. They serve different purposes, even though some information may be transferred, reused or updated between them. The aim is not necessarily to maintain one enormous model containing every piece of information from every stage.

## What is the PIM?

The PIM supports project delivery. It may include design models, drawings, schedules, specifications, calculations, programme and cost-related information, construction planning information and other deliverables required by the project. Its contents depend on the project requirements and delivery approach. For the RC building, the PIM may contain the structural model, footing design information, reinforcement details, coordinated construction information and relevant records created during delivery.

## What is the AIM?

The AIM supports the asset owner's or operator's information needs during operation and management. It may include asset identifiers, locations, attributes, specifications, manuals, warranties, inspection records and links to maintenance systems. The AIM is not automatically a detailed 3D model of every object. Its content should be based on the information the owner needs to operate, maintain, inspect, renew or manage the asset.

## Why the models are different

The project team needs information to design and construct the building. The facilities or asset management team needs information to run it safely and efficiently. Some delivery information may be irrelevant to operations, while some operational information may need to be added, validated or structured for the owner's systems. Handover is therefore a process of identifying, checking and delivering the required information, not merely copying every project file into an operations folder.

## Example: the pad footing

The PIM may contain the footing's design geometry, structural calculations, reinforcement drawings, design assumptions and construction details. During construction, the team may also generate inspection records, concrete delivery information, test results and survey records. The owner may require selected information in the AIM, such as the footing's identifier and location, relevant approved specifications, and links to construction or inspection records. The owner may not need every intermediate design file in its day-to-day asset management system, but required records should remain accessible and traceable.

## Information requirements for handover

Handover should be planned at the beginning of the project. The appointing party should identify what information is needed for operation and asset management, and the delivery team should plan how it will be produced and verified. Requirements may specify naming, identifiers, property fields, classification, formats, document links and acceptance checks. If these needs are not agreed early, the team may discover late in construction that important data was never collected or that the delivered files cannot be used by the receiving systems.

## Validation and verification

A file being delivered does not prove that its content is correct. Handover checks may confirm that required properties are populated, identifiers are unique, documents open correctly, information matches the agreed structure and records are associated with the correct assets. As-built information should reflect the verified construction condition to the extent required by the project. Any limitations, outstanding items or assumptions should be handled through the agreed process rather than hidden by labelling the model 'as built'.

## The role of open formats and systems

Information may move between authoring applications, coordination tools, document systems and asset management platforms. Open exchange formats such as IFC can support model interoperability, while spreadsheets, structured data files and document links may support other requirements. No single format is suitable for every information need. The project should define exchange requirements and test the intended workflow rather than assume that an export preserves every property or relationship automatically.

## Information lifecycle and change

Information needs continue after handover. A building may be altered, equipment replaced or structural elements inspected. The owner needs a process for updating relevant information and retaining a reliable record of changes. A well-prepared AIM can support these activities, but only if the information remains maintained and responsibilities are clear. A model that was accurate at handover can become misleading if subsequent changes are not recorded.

## Conclusion

The PIM supports the delivery of the project; the AIM supports the operation and management of the asset. Their relationship should be planned around the information needed at each stage. For the footing, the project team develops and records the design and construction information, then supplies the relevant verified information required by the owner. A useful handover is not the largest possible collection of files: it is a reliable, structured and maintainable set of information that serves a defined purpose.

## The receiving organisation should shape handover

The people who will operate the asset should help define what information they need. A model that is useful to a designer may not match the structure or fields required by an asset management system. Early engagement helps identify which identifiers, properties, documents and formats will actually be used and how they will be maintained.

## Not every project file belongs in the AIM

The project generates drafts, coordination records, temporary working files and many intermediate documents. The AIM should contain or reference the information required for asset operation and management according to agreed requirements. Other project records may still need to be retained elsewhere for contractual, regulatory or historical reasons. Selection should follow an agreed information-retention strategy.

## Handover is a process, not a single export

A successful handover includes preparation, validation, acceptance and transfer of responsibility for maintaining information. The team should test deliverables before the final milestone, resolve missing fields and broken references, and confirm that the receiving organisation can use the information. This reduces the risk of discovering after occupation that the data is incomplete or incompatible.

## Practical consideration 1

Asset information should have clear ownership after handover. The owner or operator needs a process for updating data when assets are changed, inspected or replaced. Without that process, even a well-structured AIM can become outdated and lose its value.

## Practical consideration 2

## Practical consideration 3
